source.title: The role of capacity constraints in Convolutional Neural Networks for learning random versus natural data
source.authors: Christian Tsvetkov; G. Malhotra; B. Evans; J. Bowers

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether CNNs fit random data and how capacity constraints change that ability; the models and interventions differ from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The authors cite Zhang et al. (2017) and Arpit et al. (2017) for prior results; those cited results are not rows. Figure 5 and Appendix A show noise sweeps, but precise values by noise level are not stated in the text. The rows summarize only outcomes the text explicitly describes.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures fitting randomly labeled images and Gaussian random-pixel inputs, and tests how activation noise and architectural constraints change that ability. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that pretraining preserves and accelerates random-data learning, while activation noise selectively reduces it. Bottlenecks and bounded activations modify noise sensitivity, and smaller datasets remain learnable at greater noise levels, supporting their capacity interpretation. Out-of-distribution robustness benefits are limited and condition-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: Tests CNN memorization with ResNet-50 and scaled-down architectures, and adds internal activation noise, a first-layer bottleneck, or Sigmoid activations; it does not reproduce the original methods exactly.
record.method_sensitivity: Random-data learning under activation noise varied with activation function and bottleneck; ReLU networks required about 5 times more noise than Sigmoid networks for a similar accuracy decline. Relative convergence speed between shuffled labels and random pixels varied by architecture and learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: ImageNet pretraining accelerates subsequent random-data learning, including when convolutional features are frozen.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior natural-image training can accelerate learning arbitrary image-category mappings.

fits_no_version.finding: The relative difficulty of random pixels and shuffled labels varies with architecture, learning rate and dataset size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: There is no stable ordering of optimization difficulty between these two random-data tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Small-alexnet retains relatively high accuracy on perturbed versions of random-pixel training images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitting random data can support robustness around memorized examples, without demonstrating generalization to independent examples.

record.problems: The random-data training experiments report training accuracy, not test error at chance. Several capacity-constraint outcomes are presented in figures without exact values in the text. Experiments average over four seeds for the capacity-constraint simulations; pretraining experiments use three seeds per condition. The text notes that relative difficulty of random pixels and shuffled labels was not robust across settings.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Figure-level sweeps were not split into rows for every plotted noise value because the text does not state individual values.

untested.parts: Chance test error on independent examples is not measured. The ResNet experiment does not document training hyperparameters sufficiently to verify their constancy across datasets; Section 3.2 explicitly holds them constant.
No reported time ratio establishes a small constant-factor cost relative to true labels, and no sweep of label-corruption fraction tests convergence slowing.
Shuffled pixels and independently permuted pixels are not tested; the tested unstructured inputs are Gaussian random-pixel images.
No label-corruption-fraction sweep jointly measures perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error. Activation noise is a different manipulation.
Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation and their removal are not tested. Gaussian activation noise does not directly test the named regularizers.
No within-training comparison measures shared real-data patterns being learned before noisy labels.

missing.what: Perfect-training-accuracy endpoints for fine-tuning and transfer learning on each random dataset; existing speed rows do not record these endpoints.

Reducing datasets to 10 classes with 100 examples each raises the activation-noise level required to suppress random-data learning. Record this dataset-size dependence separately; it is not merely an omitted individual sweep value.
missing.locator: Section 3.3, especially lines 423–440; Figure 5 bottom and Figure A.1 bottom

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text extraction does not preserve plotted curves, so figure-only accuracies cannot be inferred. Activation-noise failures qualify scope rather than directly challenging claims about standard unconstrained networks. No V2 verdict follows from comparisons involving pretraining or two random-data tasks.

versions.untested_parts: Test error at chance is not measured for the random-data training experiments; the text does not establish the claim under the original studies’ exact architectures and hyperparameters.
No small-constant-factor comparison is reported, and the study does not sweep the fraction of corrupted labels.
Independent pixel permutations and shuffled-pixel inputs are not tested. Random pixel images are tested; their generation is described as Gaussian-distributed color-channel samples.

rows.subject: small-inception
rows.operation_detail: Added Gaussian noise to hidden-unit activations during training and testing; increasing noise progressively reduced training accuracy on random pixel data toward chance.
rows.value: training accuracy quickly dropping to chance as noise increases
rows.note: The report describes the outcome across noise levels, activations, and bottleneck conditions; it does not give individual values in the text.
rows.check: Observed describes the intervention's effect rather than the claimed fitting effect. At sufficiently high activation noise, training accuracy reaches chance. Split the sweep: intermediate levels show partial fitting, while sufficiently high levels show absent fitting. This is a 100-epoch result with noise during both training and evaluation.

source_check.correct: Training accuracy progressively declines with increasing activation noise and reaches chance at sufficiently strong noise after 100 epochs. Restrict absent to those high-noise conditions; separate intermediate conditions from the endpoint.
source_check.problem: A single absent state overgeneralizes the chance-level endpoint to the entire noise sweep.
